title: Lammas and Lughnasa
when_text: 1 August; the hill climbs moved to the nearest Sunday, the last in July or the first in August; Puck Fair 10-12 August
intro: The first of August opened the harvest. In England it was Lammas, 'loaf mass', when bread from the new wheat was blessed in church; in Ireland, Scotland and Man it was Lughnasa, the festival of the god Lugh, with great assemblies, fairs and, later, climbs to hilltops. Many of Ireland's oldest fairs and the pilgrimage up Croagh Patrick are thought to carry on Lughnasa gatherings, though how far back is often uncertain.

facts.title: The loaf in 'loaf mass'
facts.text: Lammas comes from the Old English for 'loaf mass'. In Anglo-Saxon England 1 August was the feast of first fruits, probably when loaves from the first wheat were blessed in church; a book of charms says the Lammas loaf should be broken in four and a piece put in each corner of the barn to guard the grain.

sources.title: Lammas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The name 'Lammas' comes from Old English hlafmæsse meaning "loaf mass".

sources.title: Lammas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: a book of Anglo-Saxon charms directed that the Lammas loaf be broken into four parts, which were to be placed at the four corners of the barn, to protect the grain

facts.title: Pagan roots not proven
facts.text: The folklorist Máire MacNeill argued that the English took Lammas over from the Britons' version of Lughnasa. Ronald Hutton thinks a pre-Christian harvest feast on the date is likely, but calls a shared Celtic ritual unproven.

sources.title: Lammas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: He says it is likely "that a pre-Christian festival had existed among the Anglo-Saxons on that date".

sources.title: Lammas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: However, Hutton says that "MacNeill's thesis of a pan-Celtic seasonal ritual, like her reconstruction of pagan rites, is so far un-proven"

facts.title: A Scottish term day
facts.text: Lammas was one of Scotland's traditional quarter days until 1886.

sources.title: Lammas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Lammas Day was one of the traditional Scottish quarter days before 1886.

facts.title: Lammas lands
facts.text: Lammas lands were meadows held in strips for hay and then thrown open for common grazing from Lammas Day until Lady Day, 25 March. Leyton Marsh in east London is one that kept the name.

sources.title: Lammas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The normal day for throwing open these lands was Lammas Day (1 August) and they remained open until Lady Day (25 March).

sources.title: Leyton Marsh (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The marsh is former Lammas Land: the land was divided into strips, which were cultivated to grow hay for winter feed.

facts.title: Exeter's glove on a pole
facts.text: Exeter still opens its Lammas Fair with a procession led by the Lord Mayor, a custom said to go back over 900 years, and raises a white glove on a garlanded pole above the Guildhall while the fair lasts. The fair has moved to the first Thursday in July.

sources.title: Lammas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: During the fair a white glove on a pole decorated with garlands is raised above the Guildhall.

sources.title: Lammas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: has a processional custom which stretches back over 900 years, led by the Lord Mayor

facts.title: Funeral games for Tailtiu
facts.text: Irish legend says Lugh founded the festival as funeral games for his foster-mother Tailtiu, who died worn out after clearing the plains of Ireland for farming. Teltown in County Meath, the site of the assembly, is named after her.

sources.title: Lughnasadh (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: A story about the Lughnasadh site of Tailtin says the festival was founded by Lugh as funeral games in memory of his foster-mother Tailtiu. She was said to have died of exhaustion after clearing the plains of Ireland for agriculture.

sources.title: Teltown (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Teltown (Tailtin) was named for the Irish mythological figure or goddess, Tailtiu.

facts.title: Trial marriages at Tailtin
facts.text: The medieval assembly at Tailtin was held under a royal truce, with games, horse racing, trading, law-giving and matchmaking. Couples could make a trial marriage by joining hands through a hole in a wooden door; it lasted a year and a day. The assembly faded after the ninth century and was revived as the Tailteann Games in the twentieth.

sources.title: Lughnasadh (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: At Tailtin, young couples entered into trial marriages by joining hands through a hole in a wooden door. The trial marriage lasted a year and a day

sources.title: Lughnasadh (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: After the 9th century the Óenach Tailten was celebrated irregularly and it gradually died out. It was revived for a period in the 20th century as the Tailteann Games.

facts.title: Reek Sunday on Croagh Patrick
facts.text: On the last Sunday in July 15,000 to 30,000 pilgrims climb Croagh Patrick in Mayo, some barefoot, in honour of St Patrick's forty-day fast on the mountain. A pilgrimage there is first recorded in 1113, and it probably began as a Lughnasa gathering.

sources.title: Reek Sunday (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is likely that it pre-dates Christianity and was originally a ritual associated with the festival of Lughnasadh.

sources.title: Reek Sunday (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The earliest surviving mention of a pilgrimage at Croagh Patrick is from the year 1113

sources.title: Reek Sunday (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Between 15,000 and 30,000 pilgrims participate

facts.title: Garland Sunday and Bilberry Sunday
facts.text: Into the twentieth century Lughnasa was kept on hilltops on a Sunday near the start of August, called Garland Sunday, Bilberry Sunday or Crom Dubh Sunday, with bilberry picking, dancing, games and matchmaking. On Drung Hill in Kerry the gathering lasted until about 1880.

sources.title: Lughnasadh (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The festival persisted widely until the 20th century, with the event called Garland Sunday, Bilberry Sunday, Mountain Sunday, and Crom Dubh Sunday.

sources.title: Lughnasadh (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In Ireland, bilberries were gathered and there was eating, drinking, dancing, folk music, games and matchmaking

sources.title: Drung Hill (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Until 1880, the harvest festival of Lughnasa was held at the end of every July on the summit.

facts.title: A goat crowned king at Killorglin
facts.text: At Puck Fair in Killorglin, County Kerry, a wild goat caught in the mountains is crowned King Puck by a local schoolgirl. The fair is said to be ancient, but its record begins with a charter of James I in 1613; a Lughnasa origin is a scholars' guess.

sources.title: Puck Fair (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The fair itself is purported to be ancient but can only officially be traced back as far as 1613 when King James I issued a charter granting legal status to the existing fair in Killorglin.

sources.title: Puck Fair (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Scholars speculate that the fair's origins stem from Pre-Christian Ireland, from the Celtic festival of Lughnasa

facts.title: Yellowman and dulse at Ballycastle
facts.text: Ballycastle's Ould Lammas Fair, at the end of August, is often called the oldest fair in Ireland. Its record runs from a charter of 1606 for fairs at Dunaneeny Castle; its traditional treats are yellowman, a sticky honeycomb toffee, and dulse, a dried seaweed.

sources.title: Ould Lammas Fair (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: These include livestock and traditional foods such as yellowman, which is a local variant of honeycomb, and dulse, which is a type of edible seaweed.

sources.title: Ould Lammas Fair (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1606 Randall MacDonnell obtained a charter entitling him to hold six fairs annually at Dunaneeny Castle

facts.title: Sod towers in Lothian
facts.text: In eighteenth-century Lothian, rival bands of young men built towers of turf topped with flags, spent days trying to wreck each other's, and met in a mock battle at Lammas. In the Highlands a special cake, the lunastain, was baked.

sources.title: Lughnasadh (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 18th-century Lothian, Scotland, rival groups of young men built towers of sods topped with a flag.

sources.title: Lughnasadh (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In the Scottish Highlands, people made a special cake called the lunastain

facts.title: Bulls for a saint on Loch Maree
facts.text: Bulls were still being sacrificed around Lughnasa in the eighteenth century at Loch Maree in Wester Ross, offered to the Irish missionary saint Máel Ruba, whose hermitage was on Isle Maree; the Presbytery of Dingwall complained of the rites.

sources.title: Lughnasadh (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Bull sacrifices at Lughnasadh time were recorded as late as the 18th century at Cois Fharraige in Ireland, where they were offered to Crom Dubh, and at Loch Maree in Scotland, where they were offered to Saint Máel Ruba.

sources.title: Isle Maree (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: such as the slaughter and roasting of bulls, on an island in Loch Maree

places.name: Teltown
places.why: The site of the medieval Lughnasa assembly of Tailtiu, with its earthworks, in County Meath.

sources.title: Tailtiu (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: site of the ancient and medieval Óenach Tailtenn, a fair-like assembly held during the Lughnasadh harvest festival

places.name: Croagh Patrick
places.why: Ireland's holy mountain, climbed by thousands on Reek Sunday; there is a small chapel at the summit where Masses are said.

sources.title: Reek Sunday (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Masses are held at the summit, where there is a small chapel.

places.name: Ballintubber Abbey
places.why: Abbey founded in 1216 at the start of Tóchar Phádraig, the old pilgrims' road to Croagh Patrick.

sources.title: Ballintubber Abbey (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The abbey marks the beginning of Tóchar Phádraig, the ancient pilgrimage route to Croagh Patrick

places.name: Murrisk Friary
places.why: Ruined Augustinian friary at the foot of Croagh Patrick, near the start of the route most pilgrims take today.

sources.title: Reek Sunday (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Today, most pilgrims climb Croagh Patrick from the direction of Murrisk Abbey to the north.

sources.title: Murrisk Abbey (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: is a ruined Augustinian monastery located in County Mayo, Ireland

places.name: Drung Hill
places.why: A Kerry hilltop where people gathered for Lughnasa at the end of July until about 1880.

sources.title: Drung Hill (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: On the last Sunday of July, Domhnach na dTuras ('Pilgrimage Sunday') would be held

places.name: Killorglin
places.why: The Kerry town of Puck Fair, held every August with its crowned goat.

sources.title: Killorglin (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: annual events include the August Puck Fair festival, which starts with the crowning and parading of a "king" wild goat

places.name: Dunaneeny Castle
places.why: The ruined MacDonnell stronghold at Ballycastle where the Ould Lammas Fair is said to have begun.

sources.title: Dunaneeny Castle (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Ballycastle's famous Ould Lammas Fair is said to have started in the grounds around Dunaneeny Castle

places.name: Exeter Guildhall
places.why: The city guildhall above which the Lammas Fair glove is raised.

sources.title: Lammas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Exeter in Devon is one of the few towns in England that still celebrates its Lammas Fair

places.name: Isle Maree
places.why: Island in Loch Maree with the ruins of St Máel Ruba's chapel, holy well and wishing tree, scene of bull sacrifices on his feast.

sources.title: Isle Maree (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It has the ruins of a chapel, graveyard, holy well, and holy tree on it

places.name: Leyton Marsh
places.why: Former Lammas land in the Lea valley, where parishioners could graze animals from 1 August until 25 March.

sources.title: Leyton Marsh (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Parishioners had ancient rights to graze cattle and horses between 1 August (after the hay harvest) and 25 March.
